what: The One Rep Max Calculator estimates the most you could lift for one repetition, based on a heavier set you have already done. It uses seven published formulas: Epley, Brzycki, Lombardi, Lander, Mayhew et al., O'Conner et al. and Wathan.
It shows the average, the range across formulas and a table of training weights by percentage, with the reps most people can do at each.
uses: Many programs use percentages of your 1RM.
Compare estimates over time without max testing.
See what 75% or 85% of your max is.
tutorial: Pick kg or lb. A typed weight is converted.
Pick how to round training weights (for example 2.5 kg or 5 lb).
See the average one-rep max, Epley, Brzycki and the range.
The training table lists 50–100% with typical reps; the formulas table shows every equation.
features: Epley, Brzycki, Lombardi, Lander, Mayhew, O'Conner and Wathan.
See how much the formulas agree.
Defaults to your region and converts when you switch.

example.title: Worked example
example.text: 100 kg for 5 reps: Epley 100 × (1 + 5 ÷ 30) = 116.7 kg, Brzycki 100 × 36 ÷ 32 = 112.5 kg, Lombardi 117.5 kg, Lander 113.7 kg, Mayhew 119.0 kg, O'Conner 112.5 kg and Wathan 116.6 kg. The average is about 115.5 kg, so 80% is about 92.5 kg.

tips: Use a set taken close to failure with good form.
Sets of 3–6 reps give the most reliable estimates.
Re-estimate every few weeks as you get stronger.
Always warm up and use a spotter or safety bars for heavy lifts.
problems: A message about more than 20 reps
Use a heavier weight for fewer reps.
Check the unit; kg entered as lb gives a smaller number and vice versa.
One rep is already your max, so no formula is applied.
